title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 43–44
description: Curated B2 expressions for pleasant and unpleasant feelings, attraction, dislike, desire, and nuanced patterns of intensity and prepositions.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and exercise vocabulary; all teaching examples and notes are newly written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching sections, usage notes, exercises 43.1–43.5 and 44.1–44.5, and corresponding answer-key entries checked for core vocabulary, lexical contrasts, grammar, prepositions and register.

units.title: Unit 43 — Pleasant and unpleasant feelings
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 43. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Distinguish satisfaction, gratitude, relief, delight and sustained unhappiness using context and correct patterns.
Describe excitement, worry, anxiety, frustration, anger and emotional reactions with suitable collocations.
Use intensifiers such as really, quite, a bit and absolutely appropriately with ordinary and extreme adjectives.
Recognise positive and negative feelings and explain what causes them in original sentences.

items.example: Despite the small flat, he feels content with his life.
items.note: Predicative only in this sense: be content with something; not a content person.

items.example: A contented traveller watched the sunset from the train.
items.note: Unlike content, contented can come directly before a noun.

items.example: She is content with her decision to work fewer hours.
items.note: Use the preposition with before what brings satisfaction.

items.example: I feel grateful for the help I received during training.
items.note: Gratitude follows someone's helpful or thoughtful action.

items.example: We were grateful to the technician for finding the fault.
items.note: Pattern: grateful to someone for something; also grateful for an opportunity.

items.example: I was thankful that nobody had been hurt in the accident.
items.note: In the unit, thankful highlights relief because something bad was avoided.

items.example: The researchers were delighted when their proposal was approved.
items.note: Strong pleasure caused by good news or a welcome event.

items.example: I was delighted to hear that your interview went well.
items.note: The infinitive specifies the news or event that causes delight.

items.example: She felt miserable after several days of arguments.
items.note: An intense feeling that things are going badly.

items.example: He became discontented with his working conditions.
items.note: The opposite of contented; commonly followed by with.

items.example: Several students are discontented with the new timetable.
items.note: Useful pattern for dissatisfaction with a particular situation.

items.pt: de saco cheio de; farto de
items.example: I'm fed up with the constant delays on this route.
items.note: Informal and strong; be fed up with a person, thing or activity.

items.example: We're sick and tired of hearing the same excuse.
items.note: Strong dissatisfaction; of is followed by a noun or -ing form.

items.pt: já ter aguentado o suficiente; estar farto de
items.example: I've had enough of these unnecessary meetings.
items.note: The meaning behind fed up and sick and tired; natural with of + noun or -ing.

items.example: He felt depressed after months of unsuccessful applications.
items.note: The text contrasts prolonged low mood with brief unhappiness; the word does not by itself establish a medical diagnosis.

items.example: I felt confused by the conflicting instructions.
items.note: Not able to understand conflicting ideas, information or feelings.

items.example: I'm confused about which version of the plan is final.
items.note: About introduces what is difficult to understand.

items.section: B · Excitement, upset, anger and anxiety
items.example: After the lecture, she felt inspired to try a new approach.
items.note: An experience stimulates you to do something positive or creative.

items.section: B · Excitement, upset, anger and anxiety
items.example: The exhibition inspired me to start painting again.
items.note: Inspired to + infinitive; the active pattern is inspire someone to do something.

items.section: B · Excitement, upset, anger and anxiety
items.example: They were thrilled when they received the scholarship.
items.note: Very strong positive excitement and pleasure.

items.section: B · Excitement, upset, anger and anxiety
items.example: I was thrilled to meet the author after the talk.
items.note: Thrilled to + infinitive describes the cause of excitement.

items.section: B · Excitement, upset, anger and anxiety
items.example: The criticism left her feeling upset for the rest of the day.
items.note: An unpleasant emotional reaction, often caused by an event or remark.

items.section: B · Excitement, upset, anger and anxiety
items.example: The unexpected message upset everyone in the team.
items.note: Upset is also a verb; its past form is upset, not upsetted.

items.section: B · Excitement, upset, anger and anxiety
items.example: I always feel nervous before giving a presentation.
items.note: Uneasy excitement or worry, especially before something happens.

items.section: B · Excitement, upset, anger and anxiety
items.example: We were anxious while waiting for the medical results.
items.note: The unit emphasises fear and uncertainty, not just anticipation.

items.section: B · Excitement, upset, anger and anxiety
items.example: She is anxious about the changes at work.
items.note: Anxious about something expresses worry or uncertainty.

items.section: B · Excitement, upset, anger and anxiety
items.example: The students were enthusiastic about the new course.
items.note: Shows strong positive interest; typically enthusiastic about something.

items.section: B · Excitement, upset, anger and anxiety
items.example: My colleagues are enthusiastic about the proposed redesign.
items.note: About introduces the activity or idea that inspires enthusiasm.

items.section: B · Excitement, upset, anger and anxiety
items.example: I felt frustrated when the software kept crashing.
items.note: Upset because you cannot achieve something you want to do.

items.section: B · Excitement, upset, anger and anxiety
items.example: We were frustrated by the lack of progress.
items.note: By can identify the thing that creates the frustration.

items.section: B · Excitement, upset, anger and anxiety
items.example: He was furious when the company cancelled his booking.
items.note: Much stronger than angry; an extreme state.

items.section: B · Excitement, upset, anger and anxiety
items.example: The manager was furious with the supplier over the delay.
items.note: Furious with someone is common; furious about something also occurs.

items.example: We're absolutely delighted with the final result.
items.note: Absolutely naturally modifies the extreme adjective delighted.

items.example: She was absolutely thrilled to pass the audition.
items.note: An extreme adjective naturally takes absolutely.

items.example: The customer was absolutely furious about the error.
items.note: More natural for this extreme adjective than a bit furious.

items.example: I'm absolutely fed up with the noise outside.
items.note: Absolutely adds force to the already strong expression fed up.

items.example: I was quite anxious before hearing the decision.
items.note: With this non-extreme adjective, quite generally means rather.

items.example: I'm a bit confused by the new instructions.
items.note: A bit expresses a relatively mild degree of confusion.

items.example: I was quite frustrated by how slowly the project moved.
items.note: Quite with a non-extreme adjective often means rather.

items.example: By Friday, she was quite sick and tired of the complaints.
items.note: With an extreme expression, quite may mean completely, especially in formal speech.

items.example: The audience was absolutely thrilled by the performance.
items.note: In the unit's usage note, absolutely typically combines with extreme adjectives, unlike a bit.

items.example: I'm quite nervous about tomorrow's exam.
items.note: Degree depends on the adjective: rather with many ordinary adjectives, completely with some extreme ones.

items.example: I'm really pleased with the way the discussion went.
items.note: Flexible intensifier usable with the positive and negative adjectives taught in this unit.

items.example: Tension and frustration are both negative feelings.
items.note: The exercise classifies contented and thrilled as positive, and sick and tired, anxious, frustrated and confused as negative.

units.title: Unit 44 — Like, dislike and desire
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 44. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Express liking, affection, commitment and attraction with appropriate strength and prepositions.
Distinguish informal, neutral and strong verbs for dislike, shock, disgust and aversion.
Use look forward to + -ing, dread + -ing, desire to + infinitive, long for and yearn for accurately.
Contrast participial adjectives for feelings and their causes and avoid typical word-form and preposition errors.

items.example: Fancy that! Your old neighbour is now a famous chef.
items.note: Here fancy expresses surprise, distinct from finding someone attractive.

items.pt: sentir atração por alguém; estar a fim de alguém
items.example: She has fancied her classmate since September.
items.note: Informal British English: to find someone romantically or sexually attractive.

items.example: I quite like his latest album, although it isn't my favourite.
items.note: Usually a moderate, not extreme, degree of liking.

items.example: The history of the old building fascinates me.
items.note: Something or someone holds your attention because it is very interesting.

items.example: The children were fascinated by the strange insects.
items.note: A person feels fascinated by something; the thing itself is fascinating.

items.example: Her confidence attracted him from the beginning.
items.note: To arouse interest or attraction, not necessarily sexual attraction.

items.example: He was attracted to her sense of humour.
items.note: To identifies the person or quality that appeals to you.

items.example: I'm keen on learning to sail next summer.
items.note: Keen on + noun or -ing form in this sense; not keen in.

items.example: They fell in love with each other during university.
items.note: Fall in love with someone: an emotional development, often gradual.

items.pt: agradar a; atrair o interesse de
items.example: The idea of working abroad appeals to her.
items.note: The thing appeals to the person, not appeals someone.

items.pt: ficar encantado por; ficar cativado por
items.example: I was captivated by the speaker's storytelling.
items.note: A stronger sense of charm and absorbed attention.

items.example: The dancer's performance captivated the audience.
items.note: Transitive: the performance captivates someone; they are captivated by it.

items.pt: apaixonar-se por; cair de amores por
items.example: He fell for her as soon as they started talking.
items.note: Informal way of saying become romantically attracted to someone.

items.example: Her caring attitude makes new students feel welcome.
items.note: Describes someone who shows concern for others.

items.pt: gostar muito de; ter carinho por
items.example: I'm very fond of my grandfather.
items.note: Fond of is a warm personal liking; always followed by of.

items.example: Our dog is especially affectionate in the morning.
items.note: Showing fondness through warm behaviour, words or touch.

items.example: She is always affectionate towards her younger brother.
items.note: Towards identifies the recipient of affection.

items.example: He grew up in a loving family.
items.note: Shows love and care rather than merely expressing interest.

items.example: Both parents were loving towards their children.
items.note: Towards introduces the person receiving care.

items.example: She's passionate about improving access to education.
items.note: Strong, committed enthusiasm; can describe causes, work or people.

items.example: Volunteers care for injured birds at the shelter.
items.note: Here care for means look after, not simply find attractive.

items.example: He's devoted to his family despite his demanding job.
items.note: Very strong commitment or affection; use to + person or cause.

items.example: The explorer's mysterious past intrigued her.
items.note: The passage uses a mysterious past as a quality that attracts interest.

items.example: His dry sense of humour appealed to everyone.
items.note: A personal trait that may make someone attractive; British spelling humour.

items.example: Little by little, their friendship became more important.
items.note: A gradual development, used in the narrative about falling in love.

items.example: I loathe being interrupted while I'm speaking.
items.note: Much stronger than dislike; followed by a noun or -ing form.

items.example: She detests people who are rude to waiters.
items.note: Strong dislike; followed by a noun or -ing form.

items.example: He despises dishonesty in public life.
items.note: Strong disapproval, often with a sense of contempt.

items.example: I can't stand waiting in long queues.
items.note: Strong dislike; verb takes a noun or -ing form.

items.example: I can't bear hearing people argue over small things.
items.note: In the unit, followed by a noun or -ing; bear is the correct spelling, not bare.

items.example: His arrogance repels many potential colleagues.
items.note: A person or behaviour causes an intense negative reaction.

items.example: I was repelled by the unpleasant smell in the room.
items.note: The person is repelled by the cause; do not confuse repel with repeal.

items.example: The cruelty shown in the documentary revolted viewers.
items.note: As a transitive verb here, it means cause deep disgust or shock.

items.pt: ficar revoltado com; sentir repulsa por
items.example: We were revolted by the company's treatment of its workers.
items.note: Revolted describes the person's reaction; revolting describes the cause.

items.example: The lack of basic safety precautions appalled the inspectors.
items.note: British spelling appal, appalled; a serious feeling of shock and disapproval.

items.pt: ficar chocado com; ficar consternado com
items.example: The visitors were appalled by the state of the hospital.
items.note: Appalled means shocked and upset, not attracted; avoid appealed in this sense.

items.example: The politician's cruel remarks disgusted the audience.
items.note: Transitive verb: something disgusts someone.

items.pt: sentir nojo de; ficar indignado com
items.example: She was disgusted by the unfair treatment of her friend.
items.note: Use disgusted for the person's feeling, disgusting for its cause.

items.example: The kitchen was in a disgusting condition.
items.note: Describes the thing causing revulsion, unlike disgusted.

items.example: Bad-mannered passengers can make the journey stressful.
items.note: A typical object of loathe or detest in the source.

items.example: She has a strong desire to study another language.
items.note: Formal noun or verb for strong wanting; as a verb can also mean sexual attraction.

items.example: He has a strong desire to visit Japan one day.
items.note: Pattern: a desire to + infinitive; not a desire of doing something.

items.pt: aguardar com expectativa; estar ansioso por
items.example: I look forward to seeing the team again next month.
items.note: To is a preposition here: use a noun or -ing, not an infinitive.

items.example: We're looking forward to starting the new course.
items.note: Continuous present is especially common for an anticipated event.

items.example: She dreads travelling alone at night.
items.note: Strong negative anticipation; followed by a noun or -ing form.

items.example: I'm dreading the interview because I haven't prepared enough.
items.note: Contrasts with looking forward to; describes something anticipated unpleasantly.

items.example: After weeks away, he longed for his own bed.
items.note: Follow for with the desired person, thing or situation.

items.example: She longs to live closer to her family.
items.note: Long to + infinitive is a natural extension of the long for pattern.

items.pt: ansiar profundamente por; sentir saudade de
items.example: Even abroad, she yearned for the sounds of her hometown.
items.note: A somewhat literary or poetic alternative to long for.

items.example: He yearns to see the mountains again.
items.note: Yearn to + infinitive; the exercise contrasts it with longing to.

items.example: The history of the old city is fascinating.
items.note: The cause is fascinating; the person who experiences it is fascinated.

items.example: I was appalled at the shocking conditions.
items.note: Do not confuse appalled by/at terrible conditions with appealed to by something attractive.

items.example: I cannot bear loud music when I'm trying to sleep.
items.note: Verb bear means tolerate; bare is a different word.

items.example: She feels strongly about protecting endangered species.
items.note: Reinforces passionate about without implying romantic attraction.
